newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian inflation drops to 27-year low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian inflation drops to 27-year low.

text.p: Italy's inflation rate slowed to its lowest level for more than 27 years, national statistics institute ISTAT said on Wednesday, with October consumer price growth down at three percent year-on-year and still falling.
"Inflation is at its lowest level since June 1969 when it was 2.5 percent," said Guido Vaccaro, head of studies in Istat's inflation office in Rome.

Final figures for October showed the consumer price index at three percent year-on-year compared with 3.4 percent in September. On a monthly basis, inflation rose 0.1 percent against a 0.3 percent increase in September.
ISTAT said the main areas of slowdown were in the food and transport sectors thanks to lower seafood product prices and a price war between domestic airlines.
Vaccaro indicated he expected CPI to fall further next month, noting inflation rose a high 0.6 percent month-on-month in November 1995 to give a year-on-year figure of six percent.
"If this November the month-on-month increase is less than 0.6 percent then the year-on-year figure will be less than three percent," Vaccaro said.
"Recently we haven't had a month-on-month increase of 0.6 percent and so far we haven't had any increases in tariffs which would weigh on the month-on-month figure," he said.
Economists were also upbeat on prospects for tamer prices, forecasting November CPI at 2.7 percent.
Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said the figures showed price strength came in seasonal sectors like clothing, footwear and housing.

"Those sectors should be more subdued in the next report. If you strip out those factors and take into account the weakness of food prices which have the biggest weighting on the CPI then the prospects for the next month look pretty good," he said.

Pio de Gregorio, Italian economist at NatWest Markets in Milan, said, "The latest business surveys suggest price expectations are extremely moderate for the next three or four months. We've also seen oil related product prices falling in the last few days."

A further fall in CPI would reignite hopes for another official interest rate cut. The Bank of Italy last lowered its key discount rate 75 basis points to 7.5 percent on October 24 and its fixed term advances or Lombard rate at nine percent.
Wattret foresaw a 50 basis point cut in December once provisional CPI data was published -- providing Italy's 1997 draft budget had passed muster in the lower house of parliament.
The budget, which aims to lop 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) from Italy's projected deficit, is in the throes of approval by the Chamber of Deputies or lower house.
The process should be complete by November 14 after which it moves to the upper house.
Another factor likely to induce a rate cut is the lira. The government says once the budget is through the lower house, it will apply to return the currency to Europe's ERM currency grid.

Wattret said while the central bank might be loath to ease rates too rapidly after the last cut, "if the lira goes back into the ERM around the end of this month, that's another reason for thinking rates are coming down because the central bank will want to prevent the currency appreciating too much." $1=1,525 lire
